newsitem.title: USA: AOL reports third-quarter profit, marketing costs drop.
newsitem.headline: AOL reports third-quarter profit, marketing costs drop.

text.p: America Online Inc. Monday reported a third-quarter profit, beating Wall Street expectations of a loss, as the world's largest online service was helped by lower marketing expenses.

America Online reported net income of $2.6 million, or 2 cents a share, for its fiscal third quarter ended March 31, representing an 83 percent fall from $15.13 million, or 14 cents a share, in the year-ago quarter.
But Wall Street analysts had been predicting a loss, with an average estimate a loss of 7 cents a share for the latest quarter, according to First Call, which tracks estimates.

"They completely surprised me," said Abhishek Gami, a Nesbitt Burns Securities analyst. "This quarter proves that they can turn off marketing and it gives you profits. When they spend a little more, they get great subscriber growth."
America Online's revenues climbed to a record $456.2 million, up 46 percent from $312.3 million a year ago.

"They surprised everyone with earnings, so it's earnings from here on out," said Brian Oakes, a Lehman Brothers analyst. He said the company's marketing expenses are expected to stay modest until late summer, when it launches the next version of Americ Online, version 4.0

America Online said it held its membership relatively flat at about 8 million subscribers while working to improve access for existing members. Under a January agreement with attorneys general across the United States, the service had agreed to temporarily halt advertising and marketing efforts.

The agreement with the attorneys general, which also provided refunds for customers, was a result of consumer outrage after the Dulles, Va.-based company launched flat-rate, unlimited-access pricing in December.

A surge in demand resulted in network access problems, angering subscribers who kept getting busy signals when they tried to log on. AOL also had problems with e-mail and experienced at least one partial network outage.

Analysts also said they were pleased with the big increase in non-subscription revenues, which grew to $74.7 million, including advertising and electronic commerce revenues of $60.7 million which represented a 37 percent increase from the previous quarter.
"These are high margin, fast-growing and potentially explosive revenues," said Scott Reamer, a Cowen & Co. analyst. "The business model is working."
America Online has said it would seek to raise the proportion of revenues coming from ads and commerce vs. subscription fees.

AOL said that during the quarter, it signed up 27 new advertisers, despite it being a seasonally slow period for advertising. The company said it now has more than 180 advertisers, including companies such as Barnes & Noble Inc., American Greetings and TRW Inc.

The company also said that, as expected, member cancellations increased in January, due to the change in flat-rate pricing and access issues. But it also said member retention improved steadily as the quarter progressed.
America Online said the rates of conversion of trial memberships to full memberships and membership retention for April hit their highest levels for the past year.
It said it recently resumed marketing on a limited basis and plans to continue carefully balancing demand for the service with its ability to continue improving access.
When its members began having problems in January accessing the system, America Online announced a $350 million program to expand its network.
"As promised, we have worked around the clock to serve our existing members first and our top priority was, and still is, improving access," said Chairman and CEO Steve Case.
"At the same time, we have achieved profitability a bit ahead of schedule," Case said in a statement.
AOL reported earnings after markets closed. Earlier, its stock rose $3.875 to $51.25 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
